blocks.text: Picture a leaderboard app for a running club. It does not just show you the average finish time for your age group somewhere off in a settings page. It prints your own time right next to your age group's average, on your own personal results screen, every single time you finish a race. Getting that average onto your row, without losing your row, without turning the whole leaderboard into a two line summary table, is exactly the job transform does in pandas.

blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture, and the whole point of transform.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415544-555993993.png
1. Introduction

Back in the Aggregation lesson, right after you saw groupby().agg(), there was a promise left hanging: transform gets a whole lesson to itself later in this module. This is that lesson, and the core idea is worth stating plainly before anything else. An aggregation collapses each group down to one value. A transform returns a value for every single original row. That means the output of transform is always the exact same shape as the input you started with, never a smaller summarized table. Say that rule to yourself a few times, because it is the one thing this entire lesson keeps coming back to.

You already know the split apply combine pattern from the GroupBy lesson: split the DataFrame into groups, apply a function to each group, combine the results back together. Transform uses that exact same split and apply step. The only thing that changes is how the combine step works, and that difference is genuinely useful once you see what it unlocks.

items: The one rule that separates transform from agg, and why the output shape is the whole story.
The single most common transform pattern: broadcasting a group statistic back onto every row of that group.
Why transform beats the manual alternative of aggregating and then merging the result back onto the original DataFrame.
Built in transform functions versus writing your own, including group level z score normalization.
Filling a missing value with a group specific statistic instead of one global number for the whole dataset.
A worked example computing each order's percentage of its own region's total sales.

blocks.text: 2. Aggregate Collapses, Transform Broadcasts
Take the same call you already know from the Aggregation lesson and just swap the method name. Nothing else about the setup changes, and the difference in what comes back is dramatic.

code.content:
df.groupby('region')['amount'].sum()
# region
# east    2569.0
# west    5330.0
# Name: amount, dtype: float64      -> two rows, one per region

df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('sum')
# 0    2569.0
# 1    5330.0
# 2    2569.0
# 3    5330.0
# 4    2569.0
# 5    5330.0
# Name: amount, dtype: float64      -> six rows, one per ORIGINAL row

blocks.caption: Same call, same grouping, completely different output length.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415545-623637208.png

blocks.title: The one line test
blocks.content: If you are ever unsure whether you need agg or transform, ask one question. Should my output have fewer rows than my input, or exactly the same number of rows as my input. Fewer rows means agg. The exact same number of rows means transform. That is the entire decision, every single time.

blocks.text: 2.1 One row per group vs one row per original row

Look closely at that transform output above. The east total, 2569.0, does not show up once. It shows up three times, once for every row in the original DataFrame that happened to be an east row. The west total shows up three times too, for the same reason. Transform is not inventing new rows or shrinking anything, it is computing one number per group and then repeating that number down every row that belongs to that group.

code.content:
len(df)
# 6

len(df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('sum'))
# 6, always, no matter what function you pass in

blocks.text: 2.2 Same shape in, same shape out

This is the property that makes transform so useful in practice. Because the result always matches your original DataFrame row for row, you can assign it straight into a brand new column with a plain equals sign. No merging, no joining, no worrying about whether the row order matches up. It already does, because transform builds its result using your original index the entire time.

blocks.alt: Same shape in, same shape out
blocks.caption: Same shape in, same shape out, every time, no exceptions.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415546-750729659.png
3. The Most Common Transform Pattern: Broadcasting a Group Stat onto Every Row

Here is the pattern you will reach for constantly once transform clicks. Compute some statistic for each group, a mean, a total, a standard deviation, whatever fits your question, and then broadcast that statistic back onto every row of that group. Once it is sitting right there on every row, you can compare each individual row against its own group's number directly, which is a genuinely common piece of feature engineering.

code.content:
df['pct_of_region_avg'] = df['sales'] / df.groupby('region')['sales'].transform('mean')

# every row now carries its own sales value AND its region's average sales,
# divided together, in a single assignment

blocks.text: Read that line slowly. df.groupby('region')['sales'].transform('mean') gives you a column, the same length as df, holding each row's region average. Dividing df['sales'] by that column, row by row, tells you instantly whether a given order was above or below its own region's typical order. A value of 1.2 means that order was twenty percent above its region's average. A value of 0.7 means it was thirty percent below. You get that answer for every single row, in one line, with no separate summary table involved at all.

blocks.alt: The Most Common Transform Pattern: Broadcasting a Group Stat onto Every Row
blocks.caption: Compute once per group, then copy the result onto every row in that group.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415546-724650967.png

blocks.title: Transform keeps your original row order intact
blocks.content: You never need to worry about rows getting shuffled or realigned. transform returns its result using the exact same index as your original DataFrame, in the exact same row order, which is exactly why you can assign it straight into a new column with nothing extra in between.

blocks.text: 4. Transform vs the Aggregate Then Merge Alternative

Before transform existed in your toolkit, broadcasting a group stat back onto every row meant a two step dance: aggregate the group stat into its own small table, then merge that small table back onto the original DataFrame using the group column as the join key. It works. It is also more code, and it opens the door to a handful of mistakes that transform simply cannot make.
4.1 The manual two step version
Here is that manual approach written out in full, computing the same region average sales as above.

code.content:
region_means = df.groupby('region')['amount'].agg('mean').reset_index()
region_means = region_means.rename(columns={'amount': 'region_avg'})

df = df.merge(region_means, on='region', how='left')
# now df has a new region_avg column, but it took a groupby, an agg,
# a reset_index, a rename, and a merge to get there

blocks.text: Every one of those steps is a place a small mistake can creep in. Forget reset_index() and the merge fails because region is stuck as an index instead of a column. Forget the rename and you end up with two columns both called amount, which pandas will happily rename to amount_x and amount_y behind your back. Get the join key spelled differently on either side, region versus Region, and the merge silently produces a column full of missing values instead of raising an obvious error.

blocks.caption: More steps, more places for something to quietly go wrong.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415547-594244466.png
4.2 What transform buys you
Now compare that entire block above to the transform version, which does the identical job in a single line.

code.content:
df['region_avg'] = df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('mean')
# one line, no reset_index, no rename, no merge, no join key to get wrong

blocks.text: Transform does the broadcast for you internally. It never leaves your original index, so there is no join key to mismatch and no risk of accidentally duplicating rows the way an unclean merge sometimes can. It is less code to write, less code to read later, and less code that can break.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Aggregate then merge","transform"],"rows":[["Steps required","groupby, agg, reset_index, rename, merge","groupby, transform"],["Join key needed","Yes, must match exactly on both sides","No, uses the original index automatically"],["Risk of duplicate rows","Possible if the join key is not unique","Not possible, row count never changes"],["Lines of code","Four to five lines typically","One line"]]}

blocks.title: The merge alternative has a trap transform does not
blocks.content: If the key column on either side of a merge is not unique, or you forget reset_index on the aggregated side, merge can silently duplicate rows or throw a confusing length mismatch. transform can never do that, because it never leaves the original index in the first place, there is nothing to join.

blocks.text: 5. Built in Transform Functions vs a Custom Function

Just like agg, transform accepts a plain string name for the common statistics, and it also accepts any function you write yourself, including a lambda. The string path is fast and vectorized. The custom function path is what you reach for once a plain built in name cannot express what you are computing.

items: mean computes the group's average and broadcasts it onto every row in that group.
sum computes the group's total and broadcasts it the same way.
std computes the group's standard deviation.
count counts the non missing values in the group.
rank ranks each row within its own group instead of across the whole DataFrame.
cumsum gives a running total within each group, in row order.

blocks.alt: Built in Transform Functions vs a Custom Function
blocks.caption: Two ways in, the string path for common stats, the function path for anything custom.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415547-349010047.png
5.1 Built in names passed as strings
For anything that already has a name pandas recognizes, just pass the string. This is the fast path, and it covers a surprising amount of real feature engineering work on its own.

code.content:
df['region_total'] = df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('sum')
df['region_std'] = df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('std')
df['region_rank'] = df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('rank')
# three new columns, each one built in one short line, no lambda in sight

blocks.text: 5.2 A custom function for group level z score normalization

Sometimes what you need is not a single named statistic, it is a small formula. A common one is the z score, subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, except you want it computed separately within each group rather than across the whole dataset. A lambda handles that cleanly.

code.content:
df['amount_zscore'] = df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform(
    lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
)
# each order's amount is now expressed in standard deviations away from
# its OWN region's mean, not the overall dataset mean

blocks.text: Pay attention to what that lambda receives and what it has to return. It receives x, the entire Series of amounts for one group at a time, exactly like a custom aggregation function would. But where a custom aggregation function has to collapse that Series down to one number, a custom transform function has to return a Series of that same length back out, one z score per row in the group. That returned length is what pandas checks, and it is the real difference between writing a function for agg and writing one for transform.

blocks.alt: A custom function for group level z score normalization
blocks.caption: Subtract the group mean, divide by the group standard deviation, one z score per row.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415548-187699073.png

blocks.title: You will see this exact pattern again
blocks.content: This lambda, subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, is the entire idea behind z score normalization. The Data Normalization lesson later in this module covers it in full, including when you would normalize a column globally instead of per group. For now, just notice that transform is what makes the per group version possible in the first place.

blocks.text: 6. Filling Missing Values with a Group Specific Statistic

Back in the Handling Missing Values lesson, you filled a missing age with df['age'].fillna(df['age'].median()), one single number computed across the entire dataset and stuffed into every gap, no matter which department that person actually worked in. It works, but it throws away information you already have sitting right there in the data. If engineering skews younger than the company as a whole, filling a missing engineering age with the company wide median quietly drags that estimate in the wrong direction.

Transform fixes this cleanly. Instead of one global fill value, you compute the fill value separately within each group, so a missing engineering age gets filled with engineering's own average age, and a missing sales age gets filled with sales' own average age.

code.content:
df['age'] = df.groupby('department')['age'].transform(lambda x: x.fillna(x.mean()))

# a missing age in engineering is filled with engineering's own mean age
# a missing age in sales is filled with sales' own mean age, completely
# independently of what happened in engineering

blocks.text: Walk through what that lambda actually does. For each department, x is that department's age Series, missing values included. x.mean() ignores those missing values automatically and computes that department's own average. x.fillna(...) then fills only the gaps inside that same department's Series with that department specific number. Every other department is completely untouched by what happens here, because transform runs this function once per group, independently.

blocks.alt: Filling Missing Values with a Group Specific Statistic
blocks.caption: A smarter fill value, computed from the same group the missing row actually belongs to.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415806-561432469.png

blocks.title: A group that is entirely missing stays missing
blocks.content: If every single row in one department has a missing age, that department's mean is also NaN, so the transform fills the gap with NaN too, nothing actually changes for that group. You would want a second, more general fillna afterward as a fallback for that edge case.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Percentage of Region Total Sales

Time to put this on real numbers, using the exact same orders you already saw in the Aggregation lesson's worked example, so you can compare the two outputs directly and see the shape difference with your own eyes instead of just reading about it.
7.1 Setting up the data
First, the plain aggregate version, exactly the kind of summary the earlier lesson built. One row per region, nothing more.

code.content:
df.groupby('region')['amount'].sum()
# region
# east    2569.0
# west    5330.0
# Name: amount, dtype: float64

blocks.text: 7.2 Comparing the two outputs side by side
Now the transform version. Instead of collapsing down to two rows, it stays at six rows, and adds a new column showing what percentage of its own region's total each individual order represents.

blocks.alt: Comparing the two outputs side by side
blocks.caption: The exact same broadcasting pattern from earlier, applied to a real worked example.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415808-153641891.png

Look at what actually landed in the DataFrame. The first row, an east order worth 599.0, sits next to a region_total of 2569.0, and its pct_of_region_total works out to 23.32. That single east order made up just over twenty three percent of everything east sold across these six orders.

blocks.title: A good sanity check
blocks.content: Group the finished column by region and sum it. Each region's percentages should add up to almost exactly 100, allowing for tiny rounding differences. If they do not, something in your transform call is misaligned.

blocks.alt: Comparing the two outputs side by side
blocks.caption: Same starting data, same grouping column, two completely different shaped results.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415809-846421056.png

That is the entire lesson sitting in one small example. agg took six rows down to two, a clean summary table for a report. transform kept all six rows and handed every single one of them a number they did not have before, ready to sort by, filter on, or feed straight into a model as a feature. Same data, same groupby, two very different jobs.
8. Recap

blocks.caption: The whole pattern in one small diagram: group, transform, broadcast.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442415809-207207417.png

items: Aggregation collapses each group down to one value. Transform returns a value for every original row, so its output is always the same shape as its input.
The single most useful transform pattern is computing a group level statistic and broadcasting it back onto every row of that group.
That broadcast lets you compare each individual row against its own group's average, total, or standard deviation directly.

The manual alternative, agg followed by a merge back onto the original DataFrame, takes more code and carries real risks like mismatched join keys or duplicated rows. Transform avoids all of that in one call.
Transform accepts built in string names like mean, sum, std, and rank for the fast common case.
A custom function or lambda passed to transform must return a value for every row in the group, not a single collapsed number the way a custom aggregation function does.
Filling a missing value with a group specific statistic, like a department's own average age, is almost always smarter than filling every gap with one dataset wide number.
When a whole group is missing entirely, a group specific fill leaves that group's gaps as NaN, so keep a global fallback fillna ready for that edge case.
